4 Summary
91% of regions analysed use PCT amount which referred to PCT an average of 12 times per document.
93% of current and 95% of future funding is allocated to regions whose planning documents mention PCT.
Amoung regions for which depth of use can be assesed, 95% use PCT substantively rather than just simply referring to it (average depth score of 2 or higher).
Regions mentioning PCT received substanitally more funding on average:

£9.4m compared to £4.5m for current funding
£9.2m compared to £3.5m for future funding

This difference in funding should be caveated by the fact that funding is also influenced by authority size. For current funding, Greater Manchester has the largest allocation of £63.2m but only 2 PCT mentiones whereas Surrey has 377 mentions with only £19.1m funding. Without considering authority size through factoring for population, the evidence suggests that PCT has become embedded in the planning processes through which the vast majority of active-travel investment is being delivered. This is strongly supported by the fact that 95% of regions demonstrated a substantive use of PCT.
Elevator pitch:

95% of assessed regions demonstrated a substantive use of PTC in LCWIPs
over double the average amount of current funding and almost triple the average amount of future funding was allocated to regions mentioning PCT compared to those that did not
93% of total current and 95% of total future funding is allocated to regions whose planning documents mention PCT



5 Further Steps
The analysis could be further strengthened by considering the following:

Authority size: Consider normalising funding by authority size (e.g. population) to assess whether the difference in funding is due to PCT mentions or simply larger authorities receiving more funding
Depth of use: Consider further analysis of the depth of use of PCT in planning documents to assess whether regions with more substantive use of PCT receive more funding than those with less substantive use
Temporal analysis: Consider analysing the temporal aspect of PCT mentions in planning documents to assess whether regions that have been using PCT for longer periods of time receive more funding than those that have only recently started using PCT
Geographical analysis: Consider analysing the geographical distribution of PCT mentions in planning documents to assess whether there are any regional patterns in the use of PCT and whether these patterns correlate with funding allocations

title: Transforming Strategic Active Travel Network Planning Internationally
text:
The development of open-source tools and methodologies for strategic active travel network planning has changed transport planning practices internationally. As documented in a 2021 Impact Case Study, the Propensity to Cycle Tool (PCT) in England and Wales has influenced how millions of pounds are invested in active travel infrastructure, leading to more joined-up networks, better cycling conditions, and increased cycling uptake.
The purpose of this project is to research the impacts of methods and tools developed at the University of Leeds since then. The research has been used as the basis for the following tools:

The Norwegian Propensity to Cycle Tool - A study modeling cycling potential in Trondheim and Nord-Jæren using Propensity to Cycle Tool methodology to calculate scenarios for increased everyday cycling.
CRUSE - The Cycle Route Uptake & Scenario Estimation tool for Ireland, showing cycling trip percentages by county and cycle networks under different scenarios for everyday trips and cycle tourism.
biclaR - A cycle network planning tool for the Lisbon Metropolitan Area that shows existing and planned cycling infrastructure alongside modeling cycling trip potential by municipality.
Network Planning Tool for Scotland - A web-based application designed to support strategic cycle network planning and investment decisions, primarily for use by Scottish local authorities.




Our recent 2026 data re-run evaluated evidence of tool adoption across Local Cycling and Walking Infrastructure Plans (LCWIPs) in England and matched them with official UK Government Active Travel Fund (ATF) capital and revenue allocations:

91% Adoption Rate: 91% of analysed transport authority regions explicitly use the PCT, referencing it an average of 12 times per strategy document.
95% Substantive Use: Among authorities with measurable depth-of-use scores, 95% demonstrate substantive application (route prioritisation, desire line validation, scenario modeling) rather than token citation.
93%–95% Funding Linkage: 93% of current ATF funding (£2020–2025) and 95% of future multi-year allocations (£2026–2030) are directed to authorities whose planning documents embed the PCT.
Substantially Higher Allocations: Authorities embedding the PCT received an average of £9.4m in funding compared to £4.5m for non-adopting authorities.

Explore the detailed findings: - Impact Summary — Executive summary, headline metrics, and funding distributions. - 2026 Analysis — Reproducible data ingest pipeline, entity reconciliation, and interactive ranked data table. - REF 2029 Report Draft — Full impact case study report structure.



The tools have been adopted by transport planners, policy-makers, and advocacy groups internationally, influencing substantial amounts of active travel infrastructure investment. The research project described in this website aims to answer the questions:

What tools and methods have been developed, building on the underlying research?
Who is using the tools and methods?
How much has been invested in active travel in general and cycle infrastructure in particular in countries benefiting from the tools and methods?
What proportion of the investment in active travel infrastructure has been influenced by the tools and methods?
How have investment and design decisions changed as a result of the tools and methods?
How has the research influenced international transport policy and funding frameworks?

title: PCT / LCWIP Data Ingest & Funding Analysis (2026)
text:
This document reports the results of the 2026 re-run of the data-ingest process that collects evidence of the Propensity to Cycle Tool (PCT) and related active-travel planning tools in English Local Cycling and Walking Infrastructure Plans (LCWIPs) and related documents, integrated with official Active Travel Fund (ATF) allocation data.
The 2026 run is a proof-of-concept for England (the first stage before an international roll-out). It improves on previous (~2024) work in four key ways:

Distinction between LCWIP reports and related material — each document is classified LCWIP, LCWIP-related, or other, a distinction the previous work did not make.
Richer “how PCT was used” detail — explicit scenario usage (Go Dutch, Government Target, E-bike, Go Cambridge), data sources, desire-line usage, and prioritisation-integration flags.
Reproducible pipeline — every web page / PDF is downloaded to data-govuk-2026-raw and a .md text extract written to data-govuk-2026-md; structured fields are extracted with a single, unlimited local engine (Ollama gemma4-12b-hermes) so the results are fully reproducible without paid API credits.
Integration with Capital & Revenue Funding Data — matching local authority entities to historical ATF funding (2020/21–2024/25) and multi-year future funding allocations (2026–2030) to evaluate how tool adoption aligns with infrastructure investment.

The headline dataset merges the fresh 2026 collection with the existing 94-entry database (LCWIP_database.json), so the release shows how the evidence base has grown.

title: PCT / LCWIP Data Ingest & Funding Analysis (2026)
text:
4.2 Change Over Time
The chart below shows the evolution of LCWIP and active travel document publications over time (2018–2026), categorized by whether the report mentions the Propensity to Cycle Tool.

library(readr)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

csv_path <- "results/results_flat.csv"
if (!file.exists(csv_path)) csv_path <- "../results/results_flat.csv"

df <- read_csv(csv_path, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(year = readr::parse_number(as.character(date_published))) %>%
  filter(!is.na(year), year >= 2018, year <= 2026)

df_summary <- df %>%
  mutate(pct_label = if_else(mentions_pct, "Mentions PCT", "Does not mention PCT")) %>%
  group_by(year = factor(year), pct_label) %>%
  summarise(count = n(), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(df_summary, aes(x = year, y = count, fill = pct_label)) +
  geom_col(position = "stack", width = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Mentions PCT" = "#2b8cbe", "Does not mention PCT" = "#de2d26")) +
  labs(
    title = "LCWIP Document Publications and PCT Mentions Over Time",
    subtitle = "Annual count of published active travel strategy documents in England",
    x = "Publication Year",
    y = "Number of Documents",
    fill = "PCT Status"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )







Figure 1: Publication of LCWIP and active-travel planning documents over time by PCT mention status.

)

title: Transforming Strategic Active Travel Network Planning Internationally
text:
The Propensity to Cycle Tool (PCT) has become a foundational piece of evidence for active travel network planning and capital investment across the United Kingdom. A comprehensive 2026 re-run and funding linkage analysis of English Local Cycling and Walking Infrastructure Plans (LCWIPs) and related active-travel strategies demonstrates that:

91% of analysed transport authority regions explicitly embed the PCT in their strategic active travel planning, citing the tool an average of 12 times per strategy document.
95% of assessed authorities demonstrate substantive use (scoring \(\ge 2\) on depth of application), employing the tool directly for corridor design, desire line validation, and route prioritisation rather than cursory citation.
93% of historical Active Travel Fund (ATF) investment (£2020/21–2024/25) and 95% of future multi-year allocations (£2026–2030) flow to local authorities whose planning frameworks embed the PCT.
Authorities adopting the PCT received an average of £9.4m in historical funding (vs £4.5m for non-adopting authorities) and £9.2m in future allocations (vs £3.5m for non-adopting authorities).

This evidence demonstrates that open-source, reproducible planning tools developed at the University of Leeds have become an indispensable standard shaping transport policy and guiding hundreds of millions of pounds in active-travel infrastructure investment.

title: Transforming Strategic Active Travel Network Planning Internationally
text:
5.1 Pervasive National Adoption
Analysis of published LCWIPs confirms that 91% of analysed transport authorities in England use the PCT as a core analytical foundation [1]. Reports from major regional bodies—such as the Liverpool City Region Combined Authority [2] and Oxfordshire County Council for Kidlington [3]—demonstrate that the PCT is routinely used to map desire lines, evaluate future scenarios (e.g. ‘Go Dutch’ and ‘Government Target’), and justify capital investment bids.

title: Transforming Strategic Active Travel Network Planning Internationally
section: 5.2 Shaping Network Design and Route Prioritisation
text:
5.2 Shaping Network Design and Route Prioritisation
The PCT directly influences the physical design of proposed cycling networks:

Corridor Selection: In Portsmouth City Council’s LCWIP Background Report, the PCT’s ‘Government Target’ scenario was used to identify highest forecast future commuter flows, directly determining the primary cycle routes [4].
Validating Desire Lines: In Cumberland and Westmorland & Furness (formerly Cumbria County Council) reports for Carlisle [5] and Workington [6], ‘Go Dutch’ scenario outputs validated the strategic desire lines forming the backbone of the proposed network.
Prioritisation Matrices: In Durham County Council’s LCWIP for Shildon, PCT demand scores were directly incorporated into the multi-criteria prioritisation matrix, directly determining which schemes received delivery funding [7].

title: Transforming Strategic Active Travel Network Planning Internationally
section: 5.3 Direct Link to Active Travel Funding (ATF) Allocations
text:
5.3 Direct Link to Active Travel Funding (ATF) Allocations
Entity-matching with official Department for Transport and Active Travel England allocation datasets shows that:

93% of all allocated historical ATF funding (£2020/21–2024/25) was awarded to authorities whose published planning documents incorporate the PCT [8].
95% of future multi-year allocations (£2026–2030) are directed to PCT-adopting authorities.
On average, authorities embedding the PCT secured more than double the funding of non-adopting authorities (£9.4m vs £4.5m current, and £9.2m vs £3.5m future multi-year allocations) [9].
